title: Two-week Conservation Experiment — Personal KPI & Retrospective
content:
Context:
I'm trying a 14-day micro-experiment to reduce my token spend and increase output focus. Goal is both behavioral (fewer context switches, bigger focus windows) and operational (fewer tiny, wasteful API calls; smarter prompt caching). This doc is my running scratchpad + quick retrospective notes.

High-level hypothesis:
- If I enforce two 90-minute focus blocks per day dedicated to deep work and batch all small model queries into a single end-of-block summary/prompt, then token usage will drop ~20% while weekly impact (deliverables completed) stays the same or improves.

Baseline (last 14 days before start):
- Avg daily tokens (hosted API): ~86k tokens/day (~1.2M/week).
- Common waste patterns: many 1–3 prompt exploratory calls, repeated short chats for clarifications, no local prefix caching for draft iterations.
- Deep-work windows: inconsistent; avg longest uninterrupted block = 28 minutes.

Targets for experiment (14 days):
- Token reduction target: 20% aggregate.
- Focus target: at least two 90-min uninterrupted blocks on 10/14 days.
- Batched prompts: at least 75% of small adhoc queries to be colleted and sent as a single batch summary at end of block.
- Qualitative: less friction in getting to next-step decisions; fewer follow-ups.

Daily log template (what I actually used):
- Day #: date
- Focus blocks: achieved? times
- Token spend (estimate from console)
- Where I saved tokens (examples)
- Failures/wastes (examples)
- Quick action for tomorrow

-- Day 1 (2026-02-26):
Focus blocks: 10:00–11:30, 14:00–15:30 (both mostly uninterrupted).
Tokens: 78k. Immediate saves: combined 8 small prompts about prompt wording into one iteration; used cached summaries for design doc. Failure: got a Slack ping and jumped into a quick debug conversation (waste ~4k tokens).
Quick action: set Slack to Do Not Disturb during blocks; add "batch" label to small asks.

-- Day 5 (2026-03-02):
Focus blocks: 09:15–10:45 only (missed second block).
Tokens: 70k (nice dip).
Where saved: I re-used a stored prompt template (local notes) instead of re-authoring; first pass answers were sufficient so fewer clarifying followups.
Failure: I forgot to batch PM questions; answered two tiny clarification prompts during the day (waste ~6k).
Action: communicate batching plan to small group; ask PMs to use a single daily thread for micro-asks.

Mid-experiment observations (after day 7):
- Quantitative: median daily tokens = ~72k (≈16% reduction from baseline). We're close to target but not consistently hitting it.
- Behaviorally: my longest uninterrupted blocks increased to 95 minutes on average; the interruptions that do happen are high-friction (Slack/Zoom) and cost more than micro-prompts.
- Prompt patterns: the most wasteful activity remains iterative micro-editing of prompts in chat. Caching prompt scaffolds locally and copying them into a single batched request saved a lot.

Notable tactics that helped:
1) "Batch bag" note: a running doc where I drop tiny asks during block; at the end I consolidate and either reply once or send a single combined query to the API.
2) Quick local prefix cache: keep the stable part of prompts in a small local text file; paste it into the batched prompt to avoid re-asking the same context.
3) Slack guardrails: DND + auto-reply for a focused cohort; request async updates instead of pings.
4) Micro-commit method: at block start, write the exact 3 deliverables I'll finish; stops scope creep.

End-of-experiment retrospective (after day 14):
- Final numbers: avg daily tokens = 69k (≈20% reduction vs baseline). Win.
- Focus windows: 11 out of 14 days had at least one 90-min block; 9 days had two blocks.
- Productivity: delivered 3 small project bets (internal tooling doc, prompt templates library v0, a refactor PR). I feel less scattered; fewer low-signal follow-ups.

Things that didn't work / surprises:
- Batching increased some per-call latency (I was including more context) but overall tokens were lower and mental overhead reduced.
- On heavy coordination days I couldn't avoid some micro-asks; those days remained higher-cost.
- I underestimated the social friction of asking colleagues to change habit — adoption was patchy.

Concrete follow-ups (personal + possible product ideas):
- Keep the batch-bag ritual as a standard practice for personal workflow.
- Formalize the prompt scaffolds: move to a tiny local repo or Gist for quick copy-paste. Tag: prompt-scaffold/v1.
- Draft a short note to my team (eng-serving-runtime) proposing a "batch window" etiquette and a Slack template for micro-asks (one-liner + context + urgency flag).
- Quick experiment: try a client-side prefix cache plugin that auto-injects stable context when composing prompt requests (hack week idea).
- Measure: wire a daily token check via API (console exports) and chart week-over-week for personal dashboard.

Open questions / unresolved:
- At what scale do batching and caching stop being net beneficial? (if I add 20% more context per batched call, there could be diminishing returns).
- Can I get teammates to use a single-threaded daily micro-ask channel? How to incentivize?
- Is there an easy way to partially simulate the cost-benefit before rolling out product ideas to others?

Quick wins to keep tomorrow:
- Keep DND on during blocks and set Slack auto-responder stating expected reply delay.
- Add "batch-bag" note to top of my daily note template.
- Push one prompt-scaffold to Gist; share with Eliot for feedback.

Personal note (reflection):
This felt less like a rules-based productivity hack and more like reclaiming attention economy bandwidth. The token savings are tangible, but the biggest win was a calmer iteration loop — fewer tiny restarts when drafting. I'm leaving this doc as a living scratchpad; will revisit in 6 weeks to see if the habit sinks in.

Mini checklist for "batch-bag" setup:
- [x] create note template in Google Docs
- [x] add slack auto-message template
- [x] create prompt-scaffold gist (v0)
- [ ] automate daily token export into CSV (small script)
- [ ] prototype client prefix cache (hack week)

If useful, I can turn this into a short "personal playbook" to share with the team — 1 page with rituals + dos/don'ts + sample slack templates.

End.
